subject: Banking
title: Glass-Steagall: Splitting the Banks
description: A quick win: understand Glass-Steagall: Splitting the Banks.

hook.text: In 1933, Congress forced banks to choose: take deposits or trade securities. You could not do both under Glass-Steagall.

buildup.text: The Great Depression proved that mixing savings with speculation was dangerous. Deposits funded risky stock bets.

discovery.text: Glass-Steagall created a wall between commercial and investment banking.

twist.text: In 1999, Congress repealed Glass-Steagall. Banks merged deposits and trading again.

climax.text: The firewall lasted 66 years. When it fell, the same risks that caused the Depression returned within a decade.

punchline.text: Built a wall in 1933. Tore it down in 1999. Crashed in 2008.

details.summary: The Glass-Steagall Act of 1933 separated commercial banking from investment banking to prevent depositor money from being used for risky speculation. Its repeal in 1999 is widely debated as a contributing factor to the 2008 financial crisis.
details.whyItMatters: Glass-Steagall's separation of boring deposit banking from risky investment banking shaped modern finance for 66 years. Its repeal allowed the creation of megabanks whose complexity and risk contributed to the worst crisis since the Depression.
takeaways: Glass-Steagall prohibited banks from combining commercial and investment banking
The Gramm-Leach-Bliley Act repealed Glass-Steagall's key provisions in 1999
Debate continues over whether repeal contributed to the 2008 crisis

faq.question: Why was Glass-Steagall enacted?
faq.answer: After the 1929 crash, Congress found that banks had used depositor money to speculate in securities and sell risky investments to their own customers. Glass-Steagall forced banks to choose between taking deposits and underwriting securities.

faq.question: Did repealing Glass-Steagall cause the 2008 crisis?
faq.answer: The relationship is debated. Repeal allowed megabanks like Citigroup to combine deposit-taking with trading. However, the most problematic institutions in 2008, like Lehman Brothers and Bear Stearns, were pure investment banks not affected by Glass-Steagall.
